newsitem.title: USA: U.S. economy picks up steam, churns out new jobs.
newsitem.headline: U.S. economy picks up steam, churns out new jobs.

text.p: The unemployment rate fell back to 4.8 percent last month, the lowest in nearly a quarter century, as the economy created new jobs at a surprisingly fast clip, the government said on Friday.

The strength in the labour market, coupled with reports showing solid growth in consumers' incomes and a booming manufacturing sector, sent financial markets reeling on concerns that economic growth might pick up enough to spark inflation.

The Dow Jones industrial average, which fell as much as 120 points during the session, recovered to end off 28.57 points at 8,194.04. After rising sharply in recent sessions, the 30-year Treasury fell more than two points -- $20.94 on a $1,000 bond -- raising its yield, which moves in the opposite direction, to 6.46 percent from 6.30 percent on Thursday.
So far, the economy has managed to post steady growth without overheating. And in the meantime, Federal Reserve policy-makers have given no hint that they plan to raise interest rates anytime soon.
But the latest figures raised some fresh doubts among economists about how the Fed would eventually react.

"With jobs and income growth growing solidly and the manufacturing sector in overdrive, the Fed has to be wondering if inflation really can remain tame as the good times continue to roll," said Joel Naroff, First Union chief bank economist.

The Labour Department said the economy created 316,000 jobs in July, compared with a revised 228,000 in June. The new figures stand in contrast to the June report, which had painted a picture of a slackening labour market.
In June, the jobless rate stood at 5 percent after rising from 4.8 percent in May.
Wall Street economists had forecast that about 193,000 jobs were created outside the farm sector last month, and that the jobless rate would edge back down to 4.9 percent.

In another report, the closely watched National Association of Purchasing Management index jumped to 58.6 in July from 55.7 the month before as factories moved into high gear. A reading above 50 indicates manufacturing is growing while one below that signals contraction.
"This was a very strong reading from the nation's manufacturing sector," said Ken Mayland, chief economist at KeyCorp in Cleveland.
On the jobs front, however, economists noted that the tight labour market conditions have yet to put much upward pressure on wages.

The report showed workers spending less time on the job, with the average work week dropping to 34.4 hours from 34.7 hours. Average hourly earnings were flat, while the factory work week dipped to 41.7 hours. Overtime fell to 4.6 hours.
"Even though there's tightness in the labour market, we're not seeing upward pressure on wages," said Hugh Johnson, chief investment officer at First Albany Corp.
The employment report -- the government's first reading on the economy's pace in July -- followed a report on Thursday showing growth slowed markedly in the second quarter.

The gross domestic product, the government's broadest measure of economic activity, grew at a 2.2 percent rate in the quarter, less than half of the revised 4.9 percent rate for the first three months of the year.
But economists said that a Commerce Department report on Friday showing that personal incomes jumped 0.6 percent in June means consumers have the buying power to fuel the ongoing economic expansion.
"We're in a mode where we're going to see a pickup in the economy," said Raymond Worseck, chief economist at A.G. Edwards & Sons Inc.
In its report, the Labour Department said the services sector added 113,000 jobs in July, while retail trade contributed 65,000 jobs. The key manufacturing sector lost 5,000 jobs last month.
